locus: Sequence at 1862 Pustet: printed pp. 420-421, text-layer lines 59897-59977 and 59989-59995, under the heading Sequentia in Missis Votivis omittenda. at lines 59894-59896. FILED UNDER ANOTHER DAY: the 1862 prints this Sequence once only, inside its March sanctoral formulary Festum VII. Dolorum B. M. Virg. (running head at line 59852) which its own date-line assigns to the Friday after Passion Sunday. Its September observance carries no formulary at all - at Festa Septembris (Dom. III. - 15. 16.), lines 74314-74320, it prints In Festo VII. Dolorum ... Missa dicatur ut in alio Festo ... sub mense Martii fol. 419. That is the 1862 sending the reader to the very lines transcribed here. The 1862 also files the September day on the THIRD SUNDAY of September, which is Pius VII's 1814 placement; Pius X moved it to 15 September in 1913. The day moved and the words did not. Read from the text layer alone; this book's page images are not available to this lane.
rights_basis: Public domain in the United States because the book was first published outside the United States before the pre-1931 line, and on that ground alone. THE LINE, AND THE YEAR IT WAS DERIVED FOR. Any work first published abroad before 1931 is out of United States copyright; that is the line guidance/missals.md records from Cornell's public-domain chart as current on 1 January 2026. THE LINE MOVES EVERY JANUARY, which guidance/missals.md:249 states in terms, so it is written here as derived for calendar year 2026 and not as a standing rule: on 1 January 2027 it becomes before 1932, and a later reader must re-derive it rather than quote this sentence. Publication at Ratisbon in 1862 clears the line by sixty-nine years, so the line would have to advance to 1863 -- not before 2095 at one year a January -- before it reached this book. AND RESTORATION CANNOT REACH IT EITHER. Restoration under 17 U.S.C. 104A grants a foreign work the remainder of the term it would have had, generally ninety-five years from publication; for 1862 that ran out at the close of 1957, so there was nothing left to restore on 1 January 1996, and the Holy See's Berne accession of 12 September 1935 and Bavaria's earlier adherence are alike beside the point. THE SCAN AND ITS TEXT LAYER ADD NOTHING FOR ANYONE TO OWN. A faithful mechanical reproduction of a public-domain work is not original authorship (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)), and machine optical character recognition adds no human authorship on top of it: the Internet Archive item's own metadata names the recogniser as ABBYY FineReader 9.0 with abbyy-to-hocr 1.1.11 and the page images as Google's -- scanner google, sponsor Google, google-id E7sPAAAAIAAJ, source books.google.com -- and whichever of the two parties ran the recogniser, it was a program and not a person, so there is no author to hold a right in the text layer. It reprints Clement VIII's and Urban VIII's prohibitions on unlicensed printing of the Missal and carries the Bishop of Ratisbon's licence to Pustet of 1 September 1861; those are ecclesiastical printing controls of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries, they were never United States copyright, and no party to them claims anything now.
